title: Root-Zone Hypoxia & Waterlogging
summary: Roots require oxygen for respiration and normal water and nutrient uptake. When pore spaces remain water-filled or poorly aerated, root function can decline even though the root zone contains abundant water.
whatToLookFor: Wilt or loss of leaf posture while the medium is still wet
Slow dryback, poor drainage, or persistently saturated zones
Reduced fine-root growth, darkened or declining roots, and weak new growth
Symptoms that worsen after irrigation rather than improving promptly
confirmWith: Measure substrate moisture and track dryback across the full container or bed
Inspect drainage, air-filled porosity, roots, and irrigation frequency together
Compare affected and unaffected zones for standing water or persistent saturation
Use pathogen testing when infectious root disease remains plausible
managementPrinciples: Correct excessive irrigation frequency or poor drainage before adding more water
Restore an appropriate wet-dry rhythm for the medium and root system
Separate confirmed infectious root disease from purely physical aeration problems
Reassess new root growth because damaged roots may not recover immediately
prevention: Choose media and containers with adequate drainage and air space
Use irrigation records rather than watering only by the clock
Check emitter output and drainage uniformity
Avoid allowing runoff or contaminated solution to move between plant groups

title: Drought & Root-Zone Water Deficit
summary: Water deficit occurs when root water supply cannot keep pace with plant demand. The useful diagnostic question is not simply whether leaves are drooping, but whether the root zone is actually too dry or unable to deliver water fast enough.
whatToLookFor: Loss of leaf or petiole turgor associated with a dry root zone
Rapid container weight loss or uneven dry pockets
Marginal scorch or slowed expansion after repeated severe dryback
Symptoms that intensify during peak light, heat, or atmospheric demand
confirmWith: Measure substrate moisture at more than one depth or location
Compare irrigation volume and emitter output among affected and unaffected plants
Inspect roots for physical damage or disease that could limit water delivery
Review leaf temperature and atmospheric demand during symptom peaks
managementPrinciples: Restore water supply without converting a dry-root problem into chronic saturation
Correct blocked emitters or uneven irrigation before changing nutrition
Reduce extreme environmental demand when roots temporarily cannot keep pace
Judge recovery by posture and new growth rather than damaged leaf margins
prevention: Track dryback trends
Verify irrigation distribution routinely
Match container volume and media water-holding characteristics to plant size
Use environmental records to anticipate periods of unusually high water demand

title: High EC & Salt Stress
summary: Excess dissolved salts increase the osmotic difficulty of water uptake and can accompany tip burn, marginal necrosis, slowed growth, or root injury. Symptoms are not specific, so electrical conductivity should be measured rather than inferred from leaf appearance.
whatToLookFor: Leaf-tip or marginal necrosis developing across multiple leaves
Slowed growth or reduced water uptake despite adequate bulk moisture
Root-zone EC rising above the recent input and crop baseline
Symptoms that follow stronger feed, insufficient leaching, or concentration during rapid dryback
confirmWith: Measure input and root-zone EC using the same documented method
Review feed concentration, irrigation volume, runoff, and recent dryback
Inspect roots for secondary injury
Compare affected zones with plants receiving the same formula but different irrigation distribution
managementPrinciples: Correct the salt accumulation process rather than adding more fertilizer to burned tissue
Adjust feed strength or irrigation strategy using measured trends rather than a single visual symptom
Avoid abrupt overcorrection when plants are already root-stressed
Track new growth after root-zone conditions normalize
prevention: Record input and root-zone EC consistently
Calibrate conductivity meters
Verify irrigation uniformity
Account for source-water EC when evaluating total dissolved-salt load

title: Root-Zone pH Drift & Nutrient Availability
summary: Root-zone pH changes nutrient solubility and availability, but a pH reading does not identify a deficiency by itself. Diagnosis requires a consistent sampling method plus root condition, EC, feed composition, and symptom location.
whatToLookFor: Chlorosis or slowed growth without clear evidence that a nutrient is absent from the feed
Repeated pH measurements trending outside the crop's established working range
Differences between input solution and root-zone measurements
Symptoms appearing alongside root decline or salt accumulation
lookAlikes: Microscopic pest injury on new growth
confirmWith: Measure root-zone pH and EC with a repeatable method
Verify meter calibration before making large corrections
Review nutrient formulation and source-water alkalinity or chemistry
Inspect roots and symptom distribution before assigning a nutrient diagnosis
managementPrinciples: Correct the underlying root-zone chemistry trend instead of chasing individual leaf colors
Avoid large pH swings caused by repeated aggressive adjustment
Separate pH-driven availability problems from damaged roots that cannot absorb normally
Use new growth to judge whether the correction improved plant function
prevention: Calibrate pH meters on schedule
Record input and root-zone measurements
Track source-water chemistry
Use consistent sampling locations and timing
visualNeeds: pH problem versus root injury differential

title: Heat Stress & Canopy Overheating
summary: Heat injury is best evaluated at the tissue and canopy level. Leaf temperature can differ from room air temperature, and the most exposed leaves may experience a different combination of radiant load, humidity, and airflow than sensors elsewhere in the room.
whatToLookFor: Upper-canopy curling, edge lift, loss of posture, or scorch during the hottest period
Symptoms concentrated near high-radiant-load zones
Leaf temperature substantially different from a remote air-sensor reading
Partial recovery when light or temperature demand falls
confirmWith: Measure leaf temperature at symptomatic and unaffected canopy positions
Map PPFD, temperature, RH, and airflow where symptoms occur
Check root-zone moisture and delivery during peak demand
Compare symptom timing with fixture output and environmental cycles
managementPrinciples: Reduce the environmental load that exceeds current plant water-delivery capacity
Correct localized hot spots instead of relying only on room-average conditions
Avoid treating heat-driven curl as proof of a nutrient problem
Evaluate new growth after the canopy environment is stabilized
prevention: Measure canopy conditions at plant height
Maintain adequate but non-damaging air movement
Commission lighting and HVAC together rather than independently
Monitor high-risk upper-canopy zones during peak load
visualNeeds: Heat curl versus root wilt comparison

title: Cold & Chilling Stress
summary: Low tissue or root-zone temperatures can slow metabolism, water uptake, and growth. Chilling symptoms overlap with nutrient and root problems, so temperature history and location matter more than leaf color alone.
whatToLookFor: Slowed growth following cold nights, cold irrigation solution, or cold root-zone conditions
Temporary wilt, discoloration, or pigmentation associated with temperature drops
Symptoms strongest near cold walls, floors, intakes, or exposed outdoor locations
Recovery lag even after air temperature improves
confirmWith: Review minimum air, leaf, and root-zone temperatures
Map cold locations rather than relying only on daytime averages
Inspect roots and irrigation temperature
Compare affected plants with protected plants of the same cultivar
managementPrinciples: Restore stable temperature conditions without abrupt extremes
Do not diagnose cold-associated pigmentation as a nutrient shortage from color alone
Protect root function as well as the canopy
Assess recovery using subsequent growth
prevention: Monitor nighttime and root-zone minimum temperatures
Avoid cold irrigation shocks where practical
Identify cold-edge microclimates
Harden plants gradually when transitioning outdoors

title: Excessive Light & Photoinhibition
summary: High photon exposure can exceed the capacity of photosynthetic processes, especially when combined with heat, water limitation, or abrupt increases in light. Bleaching and upper-canopy injury should be mapped against measured light rather than diagnosed from appearance alone.
whatToLookFor: Bleaching or paling concentrated at the most exposed canopy surfaces
Upward leaf curl or reduced leaf expansion near the highest PPFD zones
A clear timeline after fixture power, height, or photoperiod intensity changed
Less injury on shaded or lower leaves of the same plant
confirmWith: Map PPFD across affected and unaffected canopy positions
Measure leaf temperature at the same points
Review the rate and timing of recent lighting changes
Compare symptoms with shaded tissue and neighboring plants
managementPrinciples: Reduce excessive exposure and correct interacting heat or water-delivery stress
Change intensity progressively when acclimation is needed
Do not use canopy bleaching as proof of a mineral deficiency
Monitor new tissue for recovery because bleached tissue may not regain normal appearance
prevention: Commission fixtures with a PPFD map
Increase light progressively after transplant or major canopy changes
Coordinate light intensity with temperature, humidity, CO2 strategy where applicable, and root water supply
Check canopy uniformity after plant height changes

title: Edema & Intumescence
summary: Edema and related intumescence disorders are non-infectious tissue abnormalities that can produce blisters, bumps, or corky areas. They are associated with an imbalance between water uptake and water loss in susceptible plants and can be confused with pests or disease.
whatToLookFor: Small blisters, bumps, or raised areas, often most noticeable on lower leaf surfaces
Older lesions becoming tan or corky
Symptoms developing during humid, low-transpiration periods in susceptible plants
No moving pest or fungal structure associated with the lesions
confirmWith: Inspect both leaf surfaces with magnification
Review irrigation timing, humidity, airflow, and nighttime conditions
Track whether new lesions stop forming after environmental balance improves
Rule out pests and infectious lesions before assigning a physiological disorder
managementPrinciples: Correct excessive or poorly timed moisture supply when it contributes to the pattern
Improve the environmental conditions that support appropriate transpiration without creating excessive drying stress
Avoid unnecessary pesticide treatment when no pest or pathogen is present
Evaluate new leaves because existing corky lesions will remain
prevention: Avoid chronic overwatering
Maintain appropriate air movement
Track high-humidity low-transpiration periods
Learn cultivar or species susceptibility before assuming lesions are infectious

title: Phytotoxicity & Spray Injury
summary: Phytotoxicity is plant tissue injury caused by chemical exposure. Droplet patterns, exposure history, affected tissue age, temperature, light, formulation, concentration, and tank contamination can help separate spray injury from pests, pathogens, and nutritional disorders.
whatToLookFor: Speckling, spotting, bleaching, scorch, or distortion appearing after a spray or chemical event
Damage matching droplet coverage or a treated canopy zone
Symptoms appearing on exposed tissue while protected tissue remains less affected
Several plants showing a similar timeline after the same application
confirmWith: Reconstruct the application history including product, rate, adjuvant, water, tank history, and environmental conditions
Compare treated and untreated plants or protected tissue
Use magnification to rule out pests and fungal structures
Track whether injury remains static after the exposure ends or continues spreading independently
managementPrinciples: Stop repeating the suspected exposure until the cause is understood
Do not treat chemical injury with additional unverified sprays
Protect healthy new growth while the plant recovers
Follow product labels and compatibility guidance for any future application
prevention: Label and clean spray equipment carefully
Test unfamiliar mixtures or conditions on limited material first when appropriate and label-permitted
Avoid off-label concentrations and incompatible mixtures
Record application conditions and tank contents

title: Herbicide Drift & Growth-Regulator Injury
summary: Off-target herbicide exposure can produce distorted, narrowed, cupped, twisted, stunted, bleached, or necrotic growth depending on the active ingredient and exposure. New growth may be especially informative, but visual symptoms alone cannot identify a specific herbicide.
whatToLookFor: Abnormal twisting, cupping, narrowing, or strapping of new growth
A spatial gradient toward an intake, field edge, neighboring treatment area, or contaminated tool path
Multiple plant species showing injury in the same exposure zone
Symptoms beginning days after a plausible drift, volatilization, carryover, or equipment-contamination event
confirmWith: Map affected plants and species against the plausible exposure direction
Review nearby applications, ventilation intake history, compost or media inputs, and sprayer history
Inspect growing tips under magnification for microscopic pests
Use laboratory residue analysis only when practical and decision-relevant
managementPrinciples: Prevent further exposure and separate contaminated equipment or inputs
Avoid adding nutrients or pesticides merely because distorted leaves resemble another disorder
Track whether healthy new growth resumes after the exposure ends
Replace severely affected material when recovery is not compatible with production goals
prevention: Keep herbicide equipment separate from crop spray equipment
Control intake and application timing around nearby herbicide use where relevant
Verify compost, manure, mulch, and other inputs when carryover risk is plausible
Maintain application and incident records
